title: Suggestion: an implementation's behaviour is not a reason to keep a counter-intuitive rule

sections.name: statement
sections.content: When the spec settles a rule and two candidates are both sound, prefer the one a reader would expect and can state simply, unless it has a real downside. What an implementation already does is evidence, not a standing contract: Reliability over Renewal (axis 5-11) protects what the spec has declared, not behaviour the spec never stated. Where an existing behaviour is wrong or needlessly counter-intuitive, the spec fixes it rather than enshrining it.

sections.name: first case
sections.content: srs#1035 (RFC-051 Rev 16): which ordered run is kept when several tie in a whole-outline replace. The spec never stated a tie rule, so srs-rust's backward-comparison tie-break is not a standing contract; a rule a reader can predict (keep the run that comes first in the new outline) is preferred unless it has a real downside.

sections.name: open questions
sections.content: Does this refine the reading of axis 5-11 in the Decision Compass, or sit beside it as a cell-level preference? What counts as an 'obvious downside' (a migration of stored data clearly does; a code change plus a pin advance probably does not)?
